title: Học phí đại học và công bằng · Discuss both views
prompt: Some people support abolishing tuition fees at public universities, while others oppose it because of the risks it could create. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

outline.purpose: Dạng discuss yêu cầu giải thích riêng vì sao mỗi phía tin lập trường của mình rồi đưa phán đoán của người viết. Trong bài này, cân nhắc trọng tâm là: Học phí là khoản phải trả hiện tại, còn lợi ích bằng cấp đến sau. Gia đình khó vay không thể chuyển thu nhập tương lai thành tiền nhập học; bỏ phí gỡ nút thắt thanh khoản cho người đã đủ học lực. Trợ cấp phổ quát còn trả thay cho gia đình vốn đủ tiền: chi nhiều chưa chắc phân phối lại nhiều. Trợ cấp sinh hoạt giúp người thiếu tiền, ngân sách giảng dạy giữ chất lượng; hai việc này khác với chỉ xóa hóa đơn học phí.
outline.content: Supporters argue that removing tuition fees can broaden access to higher education. Opponents respond that a universal subsidy also benefits affluent families who would have paid anyway. Although fee abolition removes an entry barrier, I find the case against universal provision stronger because targeted support can address both fees and the living costs that prevent completion.

paragraphs: Supporters argue that removing tuition fees can broaden access to higher education. Opponents respond that a universal subsidy also benefits affluent families who would have paid anyway. Although fee abolition removes an entry barrier, I find the case against universal provision stronger because targeted support can address both fees and the living costs that prevent completion.

Removing tuition fees can broaden access to higher education. Upfront charges can deter capable applicants whose families cannot borrow cheaply, even when future earnings would justify the investment. A student from a low-income household could accept a university place without taking an expensive private loan. The immediate constraint is therefore access to finance, not necessarily a lack of academic ability or willingness to study. However, applicants who cannot afford accommodation or transport may still be excluded, even after tuition fees have been removed.

A universal subsidy also benefits affluent families who would have paid anyway. When public money pays the fees of applicants who would enrol anyway, that expenditure changes little about access while leaving fewer resources for students whose living costs prevent attendance. A universal subsidy can therefore be expensive without being well targeted. Fee support should prioritise disadvantaged applicants, alongside maintenance grants and adequate teaching budgets. Targeted fee support reduces spending on affluent households, while maintenance grants and teaching funds protect access and educational quality. Success should be measured by disadvantaged students' enrolment and completion, alongside teaching quality, rather than by the number of fees waived.

The access argument is persuasive about financial barriers, but does not establish that every family needs a subsidy; targeted assistance therefore offers the better balance between opportunity and limited university budgets.

paragraphs.quote: A universal subsidy also benefits affluent families who would have paid anyway.
